title: How do software (SaaS) companies make money, and what matters in their cases?
description: Subscription software economics for case interviews: ARR, churn, net revenue retention, CAC and LTV, with a worked customer lifetime value.
hook: SaaS companies make money by charging customers a recurring subscription for software they host, so the business is worth what its customers will keep paying over time, minus what it cost to win them. In a SaaS case, focus on recurring revenue, how much of it you keep each year (churn and retention), and whether each customer repays its acquisition cost quickly enough.
body:
Why the model is different

Building the software is expensive, but serving one more customer costs little: hosting, support and payment fees. That gives SaaS businesses high gross margins and heavy upfront sales and marketing costs. A customer often loses the company money in the first year and only becomes profitable if they stay. So the questions are always: how many customers stay, do they pay more over time, and how long does it take to earn back what you spent winning them?

The measures that matter

MeasureWhat it means
ARRAnnual recurring revenue: the yearly value of all active subscriptions today
ChurnShare of customers (or revenue) lost in a period
Gross revenue retentionStarting ARR kept after cancellations and downgrades, excluding upsell
Net revenue retentionStarting ARR kept including upsell from the same customers
CAC and LTVCost to win a customer, and the gross profit they bring over their life

Worked example 1: an ARR bridge

An illustrative company starts the year with 1,000 customers paying $1,000 a year: $1M of ARR. During the year 80 customers cancel, 100 new customers join at the same price, and existing customers expand their contracts by $120k.

  • Ending ARR: $1M − $80k + $100k + $120k = $1.14M, 14% growth.
  • Gross revenue retention: ($1M − $80k) ÷ $1M = 92%.
  • Net revenue retention: ($1M − $80k + $120k) ÷ $1M = 104%.

New customers appear in neither retention figure. Net revenue retention above 100% means the existing base grows on its own, through extra seats and upgrades, before any new sales. Investors watch it closely because it means growth does not depend entirely on the sales team.

Worked example 2: does acquisition pay back?

The same company spent $600k on sales and marketing to win those 100 customers: a CAC of $6,000. At an 80% gross margin, each $1,000 customer brings $800 of gross profit a year. CAC payback is $6,000 ÷ $800 = 7.5 years. With 8% of customers leaving each year, many will cancel before they ever repay. ARR is growing, but the growth is being bought at a loss.

The LTV view gives the same warning in a different form. Take a monthly product at $100 a month and an 80% margin, so $80 of gross profit a month. At 2.5% monthly churn the average customer stays 1 ÷ 0.025 = 40 months, so LTV is about $80 × 40 = $3,200. Against a CAC of $1,200 that is 2.7 times, just under the commonly quoted rule of thumb of 3 times. Cutting monthly churn to 2% lifts lifetime to 50 months and LTV to $4,000, or 3.3 times CAC. Small churn changes move value a lot.

Typical SaaS case questions

  • Why is churn rising, and which customers are leaving?
  • Should we double the sales team, or fix retention first?
  • How should we price a new AI add-on or product tier? Per seat or by usage?
  • Should we push customers onto annual plans with a discount?
  • Is this company a good private equity investment?

What a strong answer sounds like

Weak: "ARR grew 14%, so the business is healthy. They should keep investing in sales."
Strong: "ARR grew 14%, but CAC payback is seven and a half years and we lose 8% of customers a year. I'd fix retention and sales efficiency before spending more on acquisition."

Common mistakes

  • Confusing ARR, revenue and cash. ARR is a snapshot of run-rate. Recognised revenue builds up over the year, and cash depends on whether customers pay monthly or upfront.
  • Treating monthly churn as small. 2.5% a month sounds tiny, but 0.975 to the power of 12 is about 0.74, so you lose roughly 26% of customers a year.
  • Using revenue instead of gross profit in LTV. Use the margin the customer actually generates.
  • Mixing customer churn and revenue churn. Losing many small customers can matter less than losing one large one. Ask which is being quoted.

Practise

1. Monthly churn is 2%. Roughly what share of today's customers will still be there in a year?

Show the answer

0.98 to the power of 12 ≈ 0.785, so about 78.5% remain and roughly 21.5% leave. A quick approximation is 12 × 2% = 24%, which slightly overstates it because each month's churn applies to a smaller base.

2. A company starts with $30M of ARR. It loses $3M to cancellations and downgrades, gains $4.5M from upsell and wins $5.5M from new customers. What are ending ARR, growth, gross retention and net retention? How much more does it need for 30% growth?

Show the answer

Ending ARR: $30M − $3M + $4.5M + $5.5M = $37M, growth of 23.3%. Gross retention: $27M ÷ $30M = 90%. Net retention: $31.5M ÷ $30M = 105%. For 30% growth it needs $39M, so $2M more, which could come from new sales or from cutting the $3M of churn.

3. A customer pays $50 a month at a 75% gross margin. CAC is $900. What is CAC payback in months?

Show the answer

Monthly gross profit: $50 × 75% = $37.50. Payback: $900 ÷ $37.50 = 24 months.

Where to practise next

The casebook has several SaaS cases: Tessera Analytics (sales team or retention?), Tallyline Payroll (annual plan discounts), CloudLedger (pricing an AI add-on) and Flowkeep (seat versus usage pricing). For the underlying logic, read unit economics.
